html:
Sol Plaatje, a journalist, cycled through the Orange Free State in the winter of 1913 to record what the Natives Land Act did to black farmers. The Act barred black South Africans from buying or renting land outside small reserves. White farmers evicted tenants who would not become servants. Plaatje, secretary of the South African Native National Congress, was subject to the Act himself.

Awaking on Friday morning, June 20, 1913, the South African Native found himself, not actually a slave, but a pariah in the land of his birth.
… Mrs. Kgobadi carried a sick baby when the eviction took place, and she had to transfer her darling from the cottage to the jolting ox-wagon in which they left the farm. Two days out the little one began to sink as the result of privation and exposure on the road, and the night before we met them its little soul was released from its earthly bonds. … they must keep to the public roads -- the only places in the country open to the outcasts if they are possessed of a travelling permit. The deceased child had to be buried, but where, when, and how?
This young wandering family decided to dig a grave under cover of the darkness of that night, when no one was looking, and in that crude manner the dead child was interred -- and interred amid fear and trembling, as well as the throbs of a torturing anguish, in a stolen grave, lest the proprietor of the spot, or any of his servants, should surprise them in the act.
